readerTitle: Customers always compare you with something. Choose what.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (과외 교사, 정리 수납 서비스, 사내 데이터 팀, 예약 소프트웨어) + 실제 연구 (Keller·Sternthal·Tybout 2002)
insight: 고객은 언제나 무언가와 비교한다. 무엇과 비교될지를 먼저 정하면 경쟁자, 기대 수준, 적정 가격이 함께 정해진다.
misconception: 포지셔닝은 우리가 얼마나 좋은지를 알리는 일이다. 비교 대상은 고객이 알아서 정한다.

sources.text: Keller, K. L., Sternthal, B., & Tybout, A. (2002). Three Questions You Need to Ask About Your Brand. Harvard Business Review, September 2002.
사례와 상황은 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Keller·Sternthal·Tybout(2002) HBR 논문이 '준거 틀(frame of reference)을 먼저 정하고, 그다음 차별점을 말한다'는 주장을 담고 있는지 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드 5에는 논지만 일반적으로 요약했고 인용문은 쓰지 않았습니다.
과외 교사, 정리 수납 서비스, 사내 데이터 팀, 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 수치나 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Same tutor, same hour, a different price that feels fair.
body: Mira tutors teenagers in math. When her flyer said *homework help*, parents compared her with free online videos and the neighbor's college kid. Many asked for a discount.
She changed one line to *exam prep for final-year students*. Same hour, same Mira. Now parents compared her with test-prep centers, and her price suddenly looked reasonable.

image.label: Two flyers for the same tutor with different headlines
image.brief: 동네 게시판에 같은 과외 교사 전단 두 장이 나란히 붙어 있음. 한 장은 "Homework help", 다른 한 장은 "Exam prep". 각 전단 옆에 말풍선으로 비교 대상(무료 영상 아이콘 vs 학원 건물 아이콘). 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should the new service describe itself?
body: Dana is launching a home organizing business. She is fastest at packing up a home and setting up the new one. Most of her first clients were families about to move.
Which line should go at the top of her website?

options.text: "A cleaning service that goes the extra mile"
options.feedback: Everyone understands it, but now she is judged against cleaners and their hourly rates. Her real strength, fast moves, barely counts.

options.text: "Moving prep for busy families: packed, unpacked, done by Friday"
options.feedback: She picks a comparison she can win: movers' packing add-ons and a stressful week off work. It narrows her audience, but it is the audience she serves best.
Accurate, but many people are unsure what that is or what it should cost. Without a clear comparison, they often fall back on the one they know: cleaners.

cards.title: The questions customers asked changed first.
body: Under the cleaning line, people asked, "How much per hour?" and "Do you do windows?"
Under the moving line, they asked, "Can you finish before the truck comes?" and "Will you unpack the kitchen first?"
Dana did the same work either way. But the words at the top decided **what she was compared with**, and that decided which questions mattered, which rivals counted and what price felt fair.

cards.title: Frame of reference
body: Your **frame of reference** is the category or set of alternatives you ask customers to compare you with.
It quietly sets three things: who your competitors are, which basics customers expect, and what price range feels normal.
Customers always use a frame. If you don't choose one, they pick the nearest familiar one, and it may not flatter you.

image.label: One product inside two different comparison frames
image.brief: 가운데에 같은 상자(서비스) 하나. 왼쪽 액자 안에는 청소 도구 아이콘들과 "$/hour", 오른쪽 액자 안에는 이삿짐 트럭과 달력 아이콘, "Done by Friday". 같은 상자가 어느 액자에 들어가느냐에 따라 달라 보이는 느낌.

cards.softwareNote: An appointment-booking tool framed as a *calendar app* gets compared with free calendars. Framed as *a front desk for small clinics*, it gets compared with a receptionist's time, and a monthly fee looks very different.

cards.title: Say what you are before you say why you're better.
body: In a 2002 Harvard Business Review article, marketing scholars Kevin Lane Keller, Brian Sternthal and Alice Tybout argued that positioning starts with the frame.
Their point: a claim like "faster" or "friendlier" means nothing until customers know *faster than what*. The frame tells them which goal you help with and which group you belong to.
Only then can a difference land. That is why the frame comes first, and the difference comes next.

cards.title: Each frame brings its own rivals and questions.
body: A frame can be a category, a moment of use, or the thing customers would do instead, such as doing it themselves.

breakdown.label: Compared with local cleaners
breakdown.detail: Customers ask: how much per hour?

breakdown.label: Compared with movers and time off work
breakdown.detail: Customers ask: can you be done by moving day?

breakdown.label: Compared with a weekend and some boxes
breakdown.detail: Customers ask: why pay at all?

cards.title: A frame is a promise.
body: Choosing a frame means accepting its basics. If Dana says *moving prep*, customers will expect boxes, tight timing and care with fragile things. Miss those, and the frame works against her.
A frame can also be too narrow. It may fit your best customers but shut out others you need.
And a frame customers don't recognize doesn't help. They simply choose their own comparison instead.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead a five-person data team at a retail chain. Other departments see you as "the people who make reports." They compare you with spreadsheets and self-serve dashboard tools, and leadership is asking whether the team is needed.
What do you change?

options.text: Promise faster reports, with a two-day turnaround
options.feedback: Speed helps, but you stay in the report frame, competing with tools that are instant and nearly free. You fight on their ground.

options.text: Present the team as decision support: you sit with one department each month on a real call, like pricing or staffing
options.feedback: Now you are compared with outside consultants and costly bad decisions, not spreadsheets. It only works if you can deliver real advice, not just charts.

options.text: Rename the team the "Insights Hub" and redesign its pages
options.feedback: A new name can signal change. But if the work and the requests stay the same, people keep comparing you with the same tools.

cards.title: Choose what you want to be compared with.
body: The frame decides your rivals, the basics you must deliver and the price that feels fair, before customers hear a word about why you're better.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence: "Customers compare us with ___." Then write the question that comparison makes them ask. Is it a question you can win?
